extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for surrendering and re‑issuing U.S. patents: what a re‑issued patent may (and may not) do, how its date and term operate, the Commissioner of Patents' authority and its limits, and when courts will review or invalidate a re‑issue (including fraud and new‑matter constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date and term of re-issued patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued patent bears the date of the original for all purposes, except as the foundation of an action for infringement. When the term of the re-issue is expressed in years, the term runs from the grant of the original; when the original was limited by the duration of a foreign patent, the re-issue is subject to the same limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and authorities cited (e.g., Whitely v. Fisher; House v. Young; Hussey v. Bradley). Practical implications: compute term from original grant when years are specified; respect foreign‑term limitations. Note the special rule that the original date rule has an exception for purposes of bringing an infringement action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights under a re-issue accrue as of the original patent's issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of all parties claiming under the re-issue, whether as against the public or rival claimants, are held to have accrued when the original patent issued, and are interpreted and enforced according to the circumstances then existing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although substantive rights are treated as having arisen at the original issue date, the surrender of the original extinguishes actions for infringement that existed at surrender and pending suits at the date of the re-issue are abated (see Jones v. Barker; Peck v. Collins). Courts apply the factual context existing at original issuance when construing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender of original patent extinguishes it and abates pending suits
rubrics_metrics.description: All rights of action for the infringement of the original patent are extinguished by its surrender, and suits pending at the date of the re-issue are abated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: plaintiffs cannot continue pending infringement suits through a surrender-to-reissue transaction; pending actions are typically dismissed or abated. (Cited authorities: Jones v. Barker; Peck v. Collins; Gaar.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's decision conclusive on identity of invention except for fraud or facial excess of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the Commissioner in granting a re-issue is generally final and conclusive as to the identity of the inventions embraced in the original and re-issued patents, and is not re-examinable in an infringement suit except where fraud in procuring the re-issue is alleged or where it is clear on the face of the patents that the Commissioner exceeded his authority (e.g., repugnancy between old and new patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts presume the Commissioner performed his duties; they are reluctant to reexamine identity questions. To impeach a re-issue one typically must show fraud or a clear facial conflict (repugnancy). Representative cases: Seymour v. Osborne; Jordan v. Dobson; Collar Co. v. Van Dusen; Birdsall v. McDonald.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may examine statutory prerequisites and Patent Office records when noncompliance appears
rubrics_metrics.description: If it appears from the papers and records of the Patent Office in evidence that the statutory requirements for a re-issue have not been complied with, it is within the power and duty of a court to hold the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Commissioner's action is presumptively correct, courts will declare a patent invalid where the record conclusively shows noncompliance with statutory prerequisites. (See Bansom v. Mayor of New York; Whitely v. Swayne.) This supports judicial review where documentation on the face of the file contradicts the legality of the re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue available only to correct inadvertence, accident, or mistake (not to add new invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutes authorize the Commissioner to amend a defective patent by re-issuing it in corrected form, but prohibit exercising that power to introduce any new invention or to cure defects that were originally intentional or fraudulent; re-issue is permitted only where the defect arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent or deceptive intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: (1) original patent must be inoperative or invalid due to defective/insufficient specification or because patentee claimed more than entitled to; (2) the error must have arisen by inadvertence/accident/mistake; (3) correction must not introduce new matter or a new invention; (4) no fraudulent/deceptive intent. Cases: Giant Powder Co. v. California Vigorit Powder Co.; Flower v. Rayner; Whitely v. Swayne.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter/new invention may be added in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue must not embrace any new matter or claim a different invention than that described in the original patent; inclusion of new matter or a different invention on the face of the re-issue shows the Commissioner exceeded his jurisdiction and renders the re-issue void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a comparison of the two patents discloses different inventions (a facial repugnancy), the re-issue is void. Courts have held that Sec. 4916 (Rev. Stat.) does not empower the Commissioner to grant a re-issue for a different invention. Representative authorities: Giant Powder Co. v. California Vigorit Powder Co.; Powder Co. v. Powder Works; Russell v. Dodge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud (actual or constructive) in procurement invalidates re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: If a re-issue was procured by actual fraud, corrupt collusion between applicant and Commissioner, or by constructive fraud (e.g., extending claims deceptively beyond the original invention to take advantage of others), the re-issued patent will be held invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish actual fraud (collusion, corrupt procurement) from constructive fraud (deceptive extension beyond original scope). Where fraud is alleged, courts may require a direct proceeding (often an equity bill) to impeach the re-issue. Cases and commentary: Swift v. Whisen; Ball v. Langles; Jordan v. Dobson; authorities showing courts invalidate patents procured by fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral attack limitations — manner of challenging re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot generally be collaterally attacked in an infringement suit; challenges are limited to showing fraud, lack of jurisdiction, or such a repugnancy that on legal construction the re-issue is not for the same invention as the original. Where fraud is alleged, the proper remedy is typically an independent proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Commissioner's decision is judicially persuasive, defendants in infringement suits cannot ordinarily re-litigate the validity of the re-issue except on narrow grounds visible on the face of the patents or by proving fraud in a separate action. See Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Wetherbee; Seymour v. Osborne; Birdsall v. McDonald.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's jurisdiction is limited and acts beyond it are void
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner is an officer of limited authority; if he exceeds the authority conferred by statute (for example, by issuing a re-issue for a different invention), his acts are void and subject to judicial invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review will strike down re-issues that the Commissioner had no power to make. Courts have repeatedly emphasized the limited statutory scope of re-issue power and invalidated re-issues that on their face exceed that scope. See Giant Powder Co.; Kells v. McKenzie; Powder Co. v. Powder Works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for courts re-examining original patent operativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may re-examine whether the original patent was inoperative or invalid (a prerequisite to re-issue) when the patents or record disclose a case where the Commissioner had no authority to act; if a court concludes the original was not defective, it may declare the re-issue void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts presume the Commissioner acted properly, they will review the operativeness/validity question where the record indicates error. If the court’s opinion differs from the Commissioner’s on that question, the re-issue can be invalidated. See Giant Powder Co. v. California Vigorit Powder Co.; Field, J.'s discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of re-issue on suits and timing (suits begun after re-issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue can affect only suits subsequently begun; suits pending at the time of re-issue are abated and cannot be continued to take advantage of the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (e.g., United States Stamping Co. v. King; Jones v. Barker) indicate re-issues do not revive or continue pending infringement suits; a re-issue may only be operative against actions commenced after the re-issue, reinforcing the surrender‑extinguishes-original rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of regularity but availability of plenary review in appropriate cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner's acts are presumed correct and final in many respects, but that presumption does not preclude plenary review where jurisdictional limits are exceeded, fraud is shown, or the patent/record on its face demonstrates noncompliance with statutory prerequisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical posture for litigants: challenge re-issue by pointing to facial defects (repugnancy, new matter), explicit record evidence of statutory noncompliance, or by bringing an independent proceeding to prove fraudulent procurement. Cases: Grant v. Raymond; Glue Co. v. Upton; Ball v. Langles.
